content: Have you ever watched an eagle dive through the sky or felt the rush of wind while riding a bicycle? Ancient Indian texts like the Vaisheshika Sutra described motion in great detail. But imagine you are sitting perfectly still on a chair right now. Are you truly at rest, or are you zooming through space because the Earth is spinning?

content.title: Earth's Motion
content.description: An animation showing a person sitting on a chair on the surface of the Earth, which is spinning on its axis and orbiting the Sun, illustrating that rest and motion are relative.

content: This brings us to the formal definition. When an object changes its position over time relative to its surroundings, it is said to be in Motion.

question: If you are sitting in a moving train, are you in motion relative to the passenger sitting next to you?
options: Yes, because the train is moving.
No, because your position relative to them is not changing.
Yes, because the Earth is spinning.

content: Look out your window and try to spot one thing at rest and one thing in motion. Understanding motion is the foundation of physics, connecting to everything from how vehicles are designed to how planets move in our solar system.
Next time you are in a vehicle, look at the trees outside. They seem to move backward. Try to explain why this happens using the concept of relative motion you just learned!

Now that we understand motion, let's look at a race between a cheetah and a tortoise. Why does the cheetah win? It covers the same distance in much less time. But what if all cars moved at the exact same pace? How would we decide who wins a race, and how do we measure this difference?

content.title: Cheetah vs Tortoise
content.description: Animation showing a cheetah and a tortoise racing on a track. A timer runs on the screen, highlighting the difference in distance covered over the exact same time interval.

content: Scientifically, the distance covered by an object in a unit of time is called its Speed. Higher speed means a larger distance is covered in a shorter amount of time.

question: Car A covers 50 km in 1 hour. Car B covers 50 km in 2 hours. Which car has a higher speed?
options: Cannot be determined without knowing the direction

content: A common mistake when calculating speed is simply dividing numbers without checking their units. Remember that speed connects distance and time mathematically (Speed = Distance / Time). Dividing 100 meters by 2 hours gives a meaningless number unless you ensure the units match!

Walk from one end of your room to the other and time yourself with a stopwatch. Now, safely run the same distance and time yourself again. Use the formula to calculate your walking speed versus your running speed!

Have you ever wondered how people measured time before clocks were invented? Thousands of years ago in ancient India, scholars used instruments like the 'Ghati Yantra' (a water clock) to measure time precisely. But what if the sky was cloudy and the sun wasn't visible for a sundial? How could you reliably measure short intervals of time?

content.title: Ancient Timekeeping to Pendulums
content.description: Visual transition from an ancient sundial casting a shadow to a water clock dripping, and finally culminating in a swinging pendulum keeping perfect, regular time.

content: To solve this, scientists discovered that objects swinging back and forth take exactly the same amount of time for each swing. This repeating movement is called periodic motion, which led to the invention of the Simple Pendulum.

question: Which of the following natural events was traditionally used by our ancestors to measure a month?
options: One new moon to the next
The movement of shadows on a sundial

content: Think about your digital watch. It doesn't have a swinging pendulum, but it uses a tiny quartz crystal that vibrates in a periodic way. The study of periodic motion connects beautifully to music (vibrating guitar strings) and modern electronics.

Tie a small stone to a piece of string. Let it hang freely, then pull it slightly to one side and let go. Count how many times it swings back and forth in one minute. Congratulations, you just built your own simple pendulum!
